title: Systems of Classification & Historical Development

branches.title: TWO-KINGDOM SYSTEM
branches.subtitle: Carl Linnaeus (1758)
branches.note: Deficiency: Grouped fungi with plants, prokaryotes (bacteria) with complex eukaryotes, and unicellular with multicellular organisms.

branches.title: FIVE-KINGDOM SYSTEM
branches.subtitle: R. H. Whittaker (1969)

conceptBreakdown.content: From Linnaeus's early two-kingdom morphology to Carl Woese's three-domain molecular ribosomal framework, biological classification has progressively refined the boundaries separating major lineages of life.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 1.1 Chronological Evolution of Classificatory Systems
conceptBreakdown.title: 1.1 Chronological Evolution of Classificatory Systems
conceptBreakdown.content: Biological classification progressed through six key chronological milestones, advancing from gross habit observation to deep molecular phylogenetics:

listPills.title: 1. Aristotle (384–322 BCE) — First Scientific Attempt
listPills.text: Plants categorized by anatomical habit: Herbs, Shrubs, and Trees. Animals categorized by red blood presence: Enaima (vertebrates with red blood) and Anaima (invertebrates without red blood).

listPills.title: 2. Two-Kingdom System — Carl Linnaeus (1758)
listPills.text: Divided life into Kingdom Plantae and Kingdom Animalia. Core Deficiency: Grouped photosynthetic autotrophs (plants) with heterotrophic saprotrophs (fungi); grouped unicellular prokaryotes (bacteria) with complex multicellular eukaryotes (flowering plants); failed to distinguish unicellular from multicellular organisms.

listPills.title: 3. Three-Kingdom System — Ernst Haeckel (1866)
listPills.text: Created Kingdom Protista to accommodate microscopic, unicellular or simple colonial organisms lacking tissue differentiation (bacteria, algae, fungi, protozoa).

listPills.title: 4. Four-Kingdom System — Herbert F. Copeland (1956)
listPills.text: Created Kingdom Mychota (later renamed Monera) to separate prokaryotic organisms (lacking a membrane-enclosed nucleus) from eukaryotic protists.

listPills.title: 5. Five-Kingdom System — Robert H. Whittaker (1969)
listPills.text: Divided all living organisms into Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia based on five fundamental biological criteria.

listPills.title: 6. Six-Kingdom / Three-Domain System — Carl Woese et al. (1990)
listPills.text: Split Kingdom Monera into Domain Bacteria (Eubacteria) and Domain Archaea (Archaebacteria) based on 16S rRNA small subunit gene sequencing, establishing the three primary evolutionary domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 1.2 Whittaker’s Five Criteria for Kingdom Assignment
conceptBreakdown.title: 1.2 Whittaker’s Five Criteria for Kingdom Assignment
conceptBreakdown.content: Robert H. Whittaker (1969) formulated the Five-Kingdom classification based on five fundamental biological criteria:

listPills.title: 1. Complexity of Cell Structure
listPills.text: Prokaryotic (lacking a nuclear membrane and membrane-bound organelles) vs. Eukaryotic (possessing a true membrane-enclosed nucleus and specialized organelles).

listPills.title: 2. Complexity of Body Organization
listPills.text: Unicellular (cellular grade) vs. Multicellular / Tissue-level / Organ-system level organization.

listPills.title: 3. Mode of Nutrition (Primary Major Lineage Distinction)
listPills.text: Holophytic / Photosynthetic (Autotrophic - Plantae), Absorptive / Saprotrophic (Heterotrophic - Fungi), and Holozoic / Ingestive (Heterotrophic - Animalia).

listPills.title: 4. Primary Reproduction Strategy
listPills.text: Asexual division, vegetative propagation, or complex sexual cycles involving syngamy, meiosis, and gametic fusion.

listPills.title: 5. Phylogenetic / Evolutionary Relationships
listPills.text: Inferred lines of common ancestry and evolutionary cladogenesis based on comparative morphology, cytogenetics, and fossil records.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 1.3 Deep-Dive Comparison of Whittaker’s Five Kingdoms
conceptBreakdown.title: 1.3 Deep-Dive Comparison of Whittaker’s Five Kingdoms
conceptBreakdown.content:
| Feature | Monera | Protista | Fungi | Plantae | Animalia |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Cell Type** | Prokaryotic | Eukaryotic | Eukaryotic | Eukaryotic | Eukaryotic |
| **Cell Wall Structure** | Non-cellulosic (**Peptidoglycan** / Polysaccharide + amino acids) | Present in some (e.g., cellulose in dinoflagellates; silica in diatoms); absent in others | Present; composed of **Chitin** ($\beta$-1,4-$N$-acetylglucosamine) | Present; composed of **Cellulose**, hemicellulose, and pectin | **Absent** entirely |
| **Nuclear Membrane** | **Absent** | Present | Present | Present | Present |
| **Body Organization** | Cellular (Unicellular / Colonial / Filamentous) | Cellular (Unicellular / Simple colonial) | Multicellular / Loose tissue (**Mycelial**) | Tissue / Organ level | Tissue / Organ / Organ System level |
| **Mode of Nutrition** | Autotrophic (phototrophic/chemotrophic) AND Heterotrophic (saprophytic/parasitic) | Autotrophic (photosynthetic) AND Heterotrophic (holozoic/saprophytic/parasitic/mixotrophic) | Heterotrophic (**Absorptive Saprophytic** or Parasitic) | Autotrophic (**Photosynthetic / Holophytic**) | Heterotrophic (**Holozoic / Ingestive**) |
| **Motility / Locomotor Structures** | Flagella (flagellin protein), gliding, or non-motile | Cilia, flagella (9+2 tubulin), pseudopodia, or non-motile | Non-motile (except zoosporic stages in Chytrids) | Generally non-motile (except motile gametes in lower plants) | Highly motile via neuromuscular systems |
